name: Lateral medullary syndrome (Wallenberg)
presentation: Sudden vertigo, vomiting and violent hiccups are followed by hoarseness and difficulty swallowing. The patient falls toward one side and has a drooping eyelid and small pupil on that side, with loss of pain and temperature sensation on that side of the face and on the opposite side of the body. Strength is normal, which surprises everyone. Neck pain in a young patient means vertebral dissection.

deficits.sign: Loss of facial pain and temperature (spinal trigeminal tract and nucleus)
Loss of body pain and temperature (spinothalamic tract)
Dysphagia, hoarseness, absent gag, palate droops to the intact side (nucleus ambiguus)
Vertigo, nystagmus, nausea, lateropulsion toward the lesion
Limb ataxia from the inferior cerebellar peduncle
Horner syndrome from the descending sympathetic fibers
Hiccups from the respiratory centers; sometimes central hypoventilation

reasoning: The lateral medulla is supplied by the vertebral artery and its posterior inferior cerebellar branch, and a wedge-shaped infarct here cuts a characteriztic set of structures. The spinothalamic tract has already crossed in the spinal cord, so body pain and temperature loss is contralateral, while the descending spinal trigeminal tract carries uncrossed facial pain fibers from the same side to the spinal nucleus, so facial loss is ipsilateral: this crossed sensory pattern is the fingerprint of a lateral brainstem lesion. The nucleus ambiguus, vestibular nuclei and inferior cerebellar peduncle are all ipsilateral structures, giving same-side bulbar palsy, vertigo and ataxia, and the descending sympathetic fibers from the hypothalamus run uncrossed through the lateral tegmentum, giving an ipsilateral Horner syndrome. The pyramid and the medial lemniscus lie medially, in the anterior spinal artery territory, and escape, so there is no weakness and vibration and position sense are preserved. This dissociation, with dramatic bulbar, cerebellar and pain-temperature signs but normal strength, is what distinguishes the syndrome from the medial medullary syndrome and from a pontine stroke, where the facial and abducens nuclei would be involved.

imagingFindings.finding: Restricted diffusion in the dorsolateral medulla, often small and missed on early CT; thin-section DWI needed.
imagingFindings.pitfalls: Early DWI can be negative in the brainstem; repeat at 24–48 h if the clinical picture is clear

imagingFindings.finding: Tapered stenosis or intramural hematoma of the V3–V4 vertebral segment on fat-saturated T1 and MRA.
Absent PICA or vertebral artery filling; cerebellar hemisphere infarct may coexist and swell.

commonCauses: Vertebral artery dissection (younger patients, neck pain)

mimics.name: Vestibular neuritis
mimics.howToDistinguish: No dysphagia, Horner or crossed sensory loss; head impulse test positive

mimics.name: Medial medullary syndrome
mimics.howToDistinguish: Contralateral weakness and proprioceptive loss with tongue palsy; no facial sensory loss

mimics.name: Lateral pontine (AICA) infarct
mimics.howToDistinguish: Adds facial palsy and deafness; vertigo similar

management: Swallow assessment before any oral intake; aspiration is the main early danger
Antithrombotic therapy; anticoagulation or antiplatelet for dissection
Monitor breathing overnight in the first days (central hypoventilation)

imagingHint.label: dorsolateral medulla at the level of the olive

examSequence: Swinging pin from one side of the face to the other and down the body: find the crossed pattern
Look at the pupils in dim light for Horner
Say 'ah' and watch the palate; test the gag
Finger-nose and heel-shin on the side of the lesion
Head impulse test and observe nystagmus direction
